questions.q: A retailer needs to predict next week’s revenue in rand for each store using historical sales and promotions. Managers will later label each prediction as above or below target. Which technique should produce the revenue estimate?
options: Regression on historical sales and promotions
questions.why: Regression predicts the numeric revenue amount. The later above/below-target label is a separate calculation using that prediction.

clues.why: The model must estimate an amount, not a group or label.

questions.hint: Identify the output required before the manager applies the target rule.
questions.analysis: Separate the prediction from the later report. Revenue in rand is a numeric target; a threshold label does not turn the underlying amount prediction into classification.
questions.trap: Choosing a technique for the downstream label instead of the requested prediction.
reasons: Classification predicts a category or band, rather than the requested revenue amount.
Regression learns a relationship between input features and a numeric target such as revenue.
Clustering groups similar stores without directly learning the requested revenue target.
Anomaly detection identifies unusual observations rather than predicting the expected revenue amount.
questions.transfer: Predicting a lease payment amount is regression; predicting whether a lease will default is classification.

questions.q: A team uses a model priced per input token. Two prompts ask the same question with different wording. Their word counts are equal, but their quoted input costs differ. Which measurement best explains the difference?
options: The number of user requests submitted
The number of complete words supplied
The number of tokens produced by the model’s tokenizer
The number of characters displayed to the user
questions.why: Token-based input pricing uses the token count for the selected model. Equal word counts do not guarantee equal token counts.

clues.why: The measurement must match the stated pricing unit.

questions.hint: Use the provider’s stated billing unit rather than a convenient text-length estimate.
questions.analysis: The scenario specifies input-token pricing. Compare tokenized inputs using the same model and price; total inference cost can also include output tokens.
questions.trap: Treating one word as exactly one token, or confusing input cost with the total bill.
reasons: Both prompts are single requests; request count does not explain different input-token charges.
A word may be represented by one or several tokens, so equal word counts can have different costs.
The tokenizer determines the model’s input units, which are used for the stated pricing model.
Character counts can be a rough proxy but are not the billing unit in this scenario.
questions.transfer: Changing languages or including code can change token counts even when the request means the same thing.

questions.q: A hiring model has high overall accuracy. One demographic group reports more mistaken rejections, but few members of that group appear in the evaluation data. What is the best first investigation?

A common threshold alone does not establish comparable error rates or fix an inadequate evaluation sample.

lessons.title: Recognize the prediction target
lessons.body: Regression predicts a numeric amount. Classification predicts a category. Clustering groups similar examples without target labels. Reinforcement learning optimizes actions using rewards. Start with the output and constraints before choosing a service.
lessons.recall: Forecast a lease payment amount: regression or classification?
lessons.exercise: A business asks for the payment amount and a high-risk flag. Separate the outputs.
lessons.solution: Predict a numeric payment using regression. A risk classification or threshold rule is a separate output; evaluate each against its actual business target.

lessons.title: Understand generative AI
lessons.body: Foundation models learn general patterns from large datasets. Prompts guide a response; tokens are model processing units. Temperature affects sampling randomness. Evaluate accuracy, safety, cost, and latency with representative use cases.
lessons.recall: Does reducing temperature guarantee factual answers?
lessons.answer: No. Lower randomness does not provide missing knowledge or guarantee truth.
lessons.exercise: A manager proposes judging a chatbot only by how fluent it sounds. Improve the acceptance criteria.
lessons.solution: Use grounded correctness, unsupported-claim rate, task completion, safety cases, latency and cost. Include representative and adversarial cases and define when human review is required.

lessons.title: Build grounded applications
lessons.body: Use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to bring relevant external evidence into a prompt. Embeddings support similarity search. Fine-tuning changes model behavior through training. Amazon Bedrock offers managed foundation model access; SageMaker AI supports ML development workflows.
lessons.recall: Does a vector database itself write the final answer?
lessons.answer: No. It retrieves similar items; a generation model creates the response.
lessons.exercise: A private document bot gives outdated answers. Describe where to look.
lessons.solution: Check document access and freshness, ingestion, chunking, retrieval relevance, then the generated answer’s grounding. Maintain source references and evaluate with held-out questions.

lessons.title: Evaluate responsible use
lessons.body: Inspect data quality, fairness, privacy, transparency and human oversight throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy alone may hide harm to smaller groups. Human review needs a clear decision owner and escalation criteria.
lessons.recall: Can one high overall accuracy prove fairness?
lessons.answer: No. Evaluate relevant groups, errors, impacts and the intended context.
lessons.exercise: A hiring model performs well overall but rejects more qualified candidates from one group. What next?
lessons.solution: Pause automatic high-impact decisions, inspect group-level errors and data, assess legal and operational requirements with owners, mitigate and retest. Preserve an auditable human review process.

lessons.title: Secure and govern
lessons.body: Identity and Access Management (IAM) grants scoped permissions. S3 stores objects; CloudWatch monitors operations; CloudTrail records supported API activity. Protect sensitive inputs and outputs, encrypt where required, and keep secrets outside prompts.
lessons.recall: CloudWatch or CloudTrail for identifying who changed a resource?
lessons.exercise: A developer places an administrator API key in a chatbot prompt. Propose a correction.
lessons.solution: Revoke and rotate the exposed secret, inspect use, move credentials to protected service-side handling, grant least privilege and enforce authorization in the tool execution path.

lessons.title: Separate storage, compute, and services
lessons.body: Snowflake stores data independently of virtual warehouse compute. Scale up for an individual resource-heavy query; scale out for concurrency. AUTO_SUSPEND sets idle delay. INITIALLY_SUSPENDED sets creation state. Cortex Search supports text retrieval.
lessons.recall: Many queued users or one memory-heavy query: which calls for scale out?
lessons.exercise: One query spills while 50 short queries also queue. Describe two separate investigations.
lessons.solution: Inspect spill and query design for the large query and test a larger warehouse. Inspect concurrency for queued queries and consider workload isolation or multi-cluster scaling where appropriate.

lessons.title: Control data access deliberately
lessons.body: Use roles with minimum privileges. Container USAGE and object privileges are distinct. Row access policies restrict rows; masking policies control visible values. Review login and query histories for the event you actually need.
lessons.recall: Hide rows or replace column values: what does a masking policy do?
lessons.answer: It controls the values visible in a column.
lessons.exercise: A regional analyst should see only their region and masked identity numbers. Specify controls.
lessons.solution: Grant necessary container and table/view access, a row access policy for region visibility, and a masking policy for identity values. Test with representative roles, including privilege inheritance.

lessons.title: Load files or stream rows
lessons.body: A stage references files. COPY INTO a table loads files; COPY INTO a location unloads data. Snowpipe continuously loads staged files. Snowpipe Streaming ingests rows. CSV options differ from JSON options; validate malformed records rather than silently losing them.
lessons.recall: COPY INTO @stage goes into or out of a table?
lessons.answer: Out: it unloads query or table data to files.
lessons.exercise: Write a plan for CSV files with a header and occasional malformed rows.
lessons.solution: Define the correct CSV format with SKIP_HEADER=1, stage the files, validate compatible COPY loads, inspect errors, reconcile loaded/rejected counts, then automate ingestion and monitor failures.

lessons.title: Recover and tune with evidence
lessons.body: Time Travel uses retained history with AT or BEFORE and supports UNDROP. Transient tables have at most one day of Time Travel and no Fail-safe. Pruning skips irrelevant micro-partitions using metadata. A warehouse local cache is lost on suspension; persisted results are a separate cache.
lessons.recall: Can an Enterprise-level edition give a transient table 90 days of retention?
lessons.answer: No. Transient table retention is limited to zero or one day.
lessons.exercise: A cold warehouse scans 42 of 18,500 partitions. Explain why, then propose a recovery for an accidental drop.
lessons.solution: Metadata pruning skips partitions that cannot match the filter, independent of a warm warehouse cache. Use UNDROP for a supported dropped table while retained history remains available.

lessons.title: Share data and orchestrate work
lessons.body: Consumers typically supply their own warehouse compute when querying shared data. Reader-account arrangements differ. Tasks execute scheduled or triggered SQL; streams track supported table changes. Partner Connect integrates selected third-party tools.
lessons.recall: Which object tracks changes, and which executes SQL?
lessons.answer: A stream tracks changes; a task executes work.
lessons.exercise: Outline a daily incremental transformation without copying the full source table.
lessons.solution: Create a suitable stream on the source, use a task to run transactional incremental SQL consuming the change set, and monitor runs. Consider initial loading, retries, deletions, and failure recovery.

lessons.title: Prepare data without leakage
lessons.body: Split by time or entity when that matches deployment. Fit preprocessing on the training partition; apply the same transform to later data. Remove post-outcome signals. For retrieval, chunk documents, embed content, and retain useful metadata.
lessons.recall: Why fit a scaler on training data only?
lessons.answer: To keep validation information out of learned preprocessing.
lessons.exercise: A churn table contains cancellation_reason recorded after the customer cancels. Decide whether to keep it and describe the split.
lessons.solution: Remove the future outcome feature. Use an appropriate time or customer split, fit preprocessing only on training, and validate using data that represents deployment.

lessons.title: Choose ML, RAG, or fine-tuning
lessons.body: Use supervised learning for labeled predictions. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant current evidence. Fine-tuning adapts model behavior; it is not a substitute for a reliable current source. Compare prompt-only, retrieval, and customization baselines.
lessons.recall: Current facts or repeated style: which need points toward RAG?
lessons.answer: Current facts, especially when source evidence must be refreshed and cited.
lessons.exercise: A policy bot cites old reimbursement rules. Outline the diagnostic sequence.
lessons.solution: Check source freshness, ingestion and metadata filters; inspect retrieved chunks; measure retrieval recall; then inspect grounding and generation. Do not start by fine-tuning stale facts.

lessons.title: Deploy with a quality gate
lessons.body: Batch Transform fits offline scoring. Real-time endpoints fit immediate responses. Asynchronous inference fits queued, longer-running requests. Pipelines coordinate preprocessing, training, evaluation, and conditional registration. Test rollout and rollback.
lessons.answer: Training fits model parameters; inference uses a trained artifact to generate predictions.
lessons.exercise: Design a nightly scoring release that must pass a validation threshold.
lessons.solution: Version inputs and preprocessing; train; evaluate on held-out data; conditionally register an approved artifact; run Batch Transform; record output location and execution lineage.

lessons.title: Operate agents and models safely
lessons.body: Monitor infrastructure and model quality separately. Ground-truth labels enable predictive-quality checks; feature drift is an investigation signal. Trace agent tool calls, latency and errors. Enforce least privilege at execution, protect secrets, and measure token costs against quality.
lessons.recall: Does stable input distribution guarantee stable model quality?
lessons.answer: No. The relationship between inputs and real outcomes can change.
lessons.exercise: An agent’s order lookup times out and sometimes repeats a purchase action. Propose controls.
lessons.solution: Use correlated traces and tool latency/error metrics. Enforce authorization outside the model, use bounded retries and timeouts, and design idempotent transaction execution. Avoid logging personal information or secrets.

lessons.title: Map AgentCore responsibilities
lessons.body: Runtime hosts agents; Gateway connects callable tools; Memory retains conversation context; Identity manages agent authentication and credentials; Code Interpreter executes generated code in a sandbox. These capabilities complement application authorization and audit controls.
lessons.recall: Which component remembers preferences across sessions?
lessons.exercise: A service agent needs isolated hosting, API tools and durable user preferences. Map the components and a verification check.
lessons.solution: Use Runtime, Gateway and Memory, with Identity where needed. Test session separation, resource authorization and user-scoped memory retrieval. Use traces to diagnose tool failures, and keep credentials out of prompts.

lessons.title: Check formats and evaluation contracts
lessons.body: Training input, inference input and model output are different contracts. Check each selected algorithm’s supported formats. DeepAR accepts JSON Lines or Parquet training data; Factorization Machines uses recordIO-protobuf. Text overlap and semantic-similarity metrics complement factual and safety review.
lessons.recall: Can supported inference JSON prove an algorithm accepts JSON training input?
lessons.answer: No. Training and inference contracts must be checked separately.
lessons.exercise: A summary looks similar to its reference but invents a payment term. Propose an evaluation and correction workflow.
lessons.solution: Use source-grounded factual assessment and human review for high-impact claims. Inspect retrieved evidence and prompts. Track unsupported claims separately from overlap, similarity, latency and token cost.

CDC — Change Data Capture
Capture committed changes rather than repeatedly copying a full source.
A pipeline records inserts, updates and deletes for downstream preparation.
HITL — Human in the Loop
A defined human review or decision point within a workflow.

CI/CD — Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery
Automated checks and controlled delivery of versioned changes.
Validate a prompt/model release and roll back if acceptance metrics fail.
Epoch / step / batch
An epoch is a dataset pass; a step is a parameter update; a batch groups examples.

Whether generated claims are supported by the supplied evidence.
